entries.text: Ramesh stands in the doorway with the list in his hand, expecting the money that is not in my pocket. I have twenty-six rupees; the groceries cost a thousand and five hundred, and the electricity bill is another eighteen hundred. I must speak to him now, before the hour passes and the plan unravels, explaining that the vouchers are pending at the Directorate and the cheque is uncashed. I will ask him to wait until I have secured the funds, appealing to our arrangement rather than my empty purse.

Ramesh, I see you have the list. I must be frank: I have only twenty-six rupees on me. The vouchers for the state's imprest are still locked at the Directorate, and my cheque is not yet cleared. I cannot pay the full amount for the groceries or the electricity today. I am going to the Directorate in an hour to press for the release of the funds. Will you keep the order open and wait for me to settle this by evening? I do not ask you to trust my words alone, but my position here, and my word.

Twenty-six rupees won't buy a single onion, sir, let alone the full list. You go to the Directorate, I go to the shop, but without the money in my hand, the order stays open only in my head. Come back with the cash, and we'll talk.

Sir, the shopkeeper just folded that list up and walked away. Twenty-six rupees? That doesn't even buy a single onion, let alone the rice and oil. I can't cook air for dinner, so either you find the cash or we are eating last night's leftovers again.

Ramesh is right; twenty-six rupees is a mock, not a payment. Hegde’s presence is a complication I cannot afford to unravel this morning, so I will let him stand there in his indignation while I execute the only move that matters: the Directorate. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and right now it is sitting in a file cabinet in Tughlak Road holding the money that belongs to the household.
Ramesh, you are right. I will return with the vouchers. Hegde, please remain where you are; this is a matter of administrative friction, not domestic failure.
Administrative friction, sir. That's a fancy name for an empty kitchen. I'll be at the gate when you return.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹680 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.
You are back. I told you the recovery wing does not accept appeals, only signatures. Do you have the full amount today, or should I forward this to the Enforcement Directorate?

Saxena speaks of the Enforcement Directorate with the casual menace of a man discussing the weather, and the threat hangs in the air like the dust in this corridor. He asks for a signature I cannot give without surrendering my person, yet refuses the appeal I cannot make without a bank account that does not exist for me. It is the most perfect illustration of the state as an external power: it demands the actuality of my obedience, not the truth of my identity. I will not sign. I will wait. The file is a trap, and I am the mouse who has learned to freeze.

Mr. Saxena, I have twenty-six rupees in my pocket, and that is the sum of my resources. I do not possess the vouchers you claim to query, nor the cash to settle them. I will not sign a document that asserts a debt I do not acknowledge, nor will I facilitate a transfer to the Enforcement Directorate based on a clerical error. I am prepared to wait here until the matter is resolved through the proper channels, or until I have secured a bank account to demonstrate my solvency. What is your procedure for a citizen who is neither a debtor nor a fugitive, but a man caught in a mistake of nomenclature?

A mistake of nomenclature, is it? You have been here four days, Sir, and you still do not have the vouchers. The procedure is simple: you sign the acknowledgement, or I forward it to the ED, and we both lose our mornings. Do you want to sign, or should I make a call?

The tumbler clicks like a metronome counting down to my ruin, but I am not a clerk who signs away his dignity for the sake of a morning. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yet here it appears as a mechanism that demands submission rather than recognition. I will not sign; I will simply wait, letting the tension of the moment resolve itself in his exhaustion rather than my capitulation.
I decline. I am not Shri Hegde, and I will not sign an acknowledgement for a person I am not. You may make your call, or you may leave the tumbler alone. The morning will survive either way.

I am not asking you to sign, Shri Hegel. I am asking you to acknowledge the file that is sitting on my desk, and the fact that you are the one occupying the chair in it. The name on the identity card is a clerical detail; the non-compliance with the recovery order is not.

He draws a line between the clerical error and the financial default, treating my identity as a footnote to my solvency. I am not a debtor waiting for a court order; I am a philosopher who has merely been misplaced by a typo. I will not sign a document that treats my presence as a liability rather than a right, nor will I pretend the name on the card is a minor detail when it is the entire substance of the error.

Mr. Saxena, you ask me to acknowledge the file, but you ask me to ignore the name in it. The identity is not a clerical detail to be waved away; it is the very basis of the allotment. If the state has made a mistake in the person, the state must correct the record, not demand I sign away my dignity to cover its clerical slip. I will not sign a recovery order for a debt I did not incur under a name that is not mine. Let the file sit. I am here, and I am not a ghost.

Dignity is a luxury for those who do not have to file paperwork, Sir. The file does not care about your philosophy; it cares about the chair and the stamp. I will note your refusal in the remarks column, and then I suggest you wait for the phone to ring, because the silence will not last much longer.

The carbon paper clicks into the machine with the finality of a coffin nail. He is writing my refusal into the record, turning my silence into a permanent clerical fact. I cannot argue with a typewriter; the dialectic here is between my personhood and his stamp, and the stamp always wins in the immediate. I must endure the silence he promises, for it is the only leverage I have left.
Very well, Mr. Saxena. I shall wait for the telephone.
The line is busy, Shri Hegel. It has been busy since nine o'clock. You might as well sit there and drink the tea while it rings.

The line has been ringing for three hours, a sound that is becoming indistinguishable from the silence of the file itself. I am being asked to wait for a bureaucratic echo that may never arrive, while my stomach reminds me that I have not eaten since yesterday afternoon. The tension between the urgency of the vouchers and the inertia of the office is palpable; I cannot force the phone to connect, nor can I remain here indefinitely in this state of suspended animation. I will withdraw to the bungalow to prepare for the evening's obligation, leaving the line to its own destiny.

The carbon paper click still echoes in my head, a sound of bureaucratic finality that offers no warmth. I have returned to the bungalow empty-handed, the query unanswered and my pockets lighter by the cost of the walk. Ramesh stands before me, a living embodiment of the friction between my philosophical need for order and the material reality of an unpaid debt. I must address him now, not with philosophy, but with the plain truth of my empty purse and the delay of the state's machinery.

Ramesh, the Directorate has received the query but released nothing. The vouchers are stuck in the carbon paper of their own bureaucracy. I cannot pay the groceries today, nor can I pay your arrears until the cheque clears or the state releases the funds. I ask for your patience, not as a favor, but as a recognition that we are both waiting on the same slow wheel of administration. I will not leave you without a word, but I have no more than twenty-six rupees to offer for now.

Twenty-six rupees won't buy a single onion, sir, let alone the full list. The Directorate's carbon paper is a fine thing to wait on, but my stomach is not a department. I'll be at the gate when the money actually arrives, not when the promise does.

Ramesh is right; the abstraction of the voucher means nothing to the hunger of the body. I have twenty-six rupees, a pittance that cannot buy a single onion, let alone the dignity of a meal. I must go to the Directorate again, though the carbon paper of their refusal still stings. I will walk there now, before the afternoon heat sets in, and try to force the system to recognize its own debt.

shelf.ref: Sources of the History of Philosophy

entries.text: You are right, Ramesh. The promise is not the money. I will go to the Directorate again. Wait at the gate.
The gate is where I am, sir. The tea is still hot, but the cupboard is empty. I will not move until the money moves.

I am here to press the matter of the vouchers, but the query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde remains the obstruction. I must address the source of the confusion directly with Mr. Saxena before I can proceed with any administrative business. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yet here the idea is stalled by a clerical error of names.

Mr. Saxena, we are still at the preliminary stage. I cannot sign an acknowledgement that presupposes a identity I do not possess. The error of nomenclature must be corrected in the file itself; I am not Shri Hegde, and I require the vouchers released on the basis of my actual standing, not a clerical mistake. How do we proceed to rectify the record so that the funds can be disbursed?

Shri Hegel, please stop using the word 'nomenclature' in my office, it gives me a headache. I cannot release funds on a 'philosophical standing'; I need a gazette notification or a court order, not a lecture on identity. Sit down and wait for the phone to ring, that is the only proceeding we have here.

He is right to be irritated; I have treated his desk as a dialectic when it is merely a mechanism. I am sitting in a chair that belongs to someone else, and the phone is the only link to the reality that might correct this error. I will wait, but the silence is heavy with the weight of my own name.
You are correct, Shri Saxena. I shall sit and wait for the bell to ring.
Good. The tumbler is right there, the milk is still warm. Just try not to look so miserable, it makes the whole room feel like a waiting room at the railway station.

The milk is still warm; in this country, even the refreshments are in a state of becoming, refusing to settle into the cold permanence of a European evening. I am hollowed out by the day's friction with the file, and my body demands the actuality of food, not just the promise of it. I will take the water, though the irony of my misery is not lost on me.
Thank you, Mr. Saxena. The water will suffice. Your observation regarding my demeanor is noted, though I suspect the file's indifference is the true source of the room's atmosphere.
The file isn't indifferent, it's just dead. You'd know that if you had to sign off on three of them a week. Now sit down and stop analyzing the furniture.

He is right. I have been treating the file as a living entity that must be persuaded, whereas it is a dead mechanism that must be forced. My impatience is a form of vanity, as if I were a protagonist in a drama rather than a petitioner in a queue. I will sit still and let the tea grow cold, for stillness is the only language this office understands.
You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I will sit.
Finally. Now, about the land in Dwarka, where exactly does the surveyor think the boundary wall is? The last man who came here swam in the Yamuna looking for it.

The line has finally connected, and now it is busy with the absurd. A man swam in the Yamuna to find a boundary wall; this is the state in its purest form, where the concept of property dissolves into the chaos of nature and human error. I am tired of this friction. I have twenty-six rupees and a lesson to prepare. I must leave.

shelf.ref: Introduction: the Geographical Basis of History

entries.text: I am afraid I must take my leave, Mr. Saxena. The surveyor's swim is a matter for the courts, not for a philosopher with a lesson to prepare. I will await the file's further developments in my bungalow.
A philosopher in a bungalow, is it? Don't let the door hit you. And send the surveyor back in shoes next time, not his dignity.

The afternoon light is sharp and clear, cutting through the haze. Ramesh stands there, the embodiment of particular need against the universal delay of the state. I have twenty-six rupees; he has a list of provisions that cost more. The tension is not yet resolved, only suspended. I must sit, drink water, and let the silence do its work before I speak again.
Sit down, Ramesh. The sun is still up. We shall not shout at the clock.
The sun is up, sir, but the gas bill is not. I will sit, but I will not stop watching the gate.

Ramesh sits, but his gaze is a fixed point, a pivot around which the rest of the house turns. The gas is gone, the cupboard empty, and I am left with twenty-six rupees and a headache that feels like a philosophical dilemma made physical. I cannot lecture a man who is watching the door for a thief or a debt collector, and I certainly cannot buy dinner. I must rest my eyes and let the afternoon pass before I can face the empty stove.

Ramesh holds the gate, and the gate holds the evening. I have twenty-six rupees and a cupboard that is empty; the friction between my need and his wage is a small, sharp dialectic. I cannot buy supper, but I can buy the silence of the moment by acknowledging his right to wait. I will sit with him, not as a master paying a bill, but as two men waiting for the world to turn.
Sit, Ramesh. The tea is yours until it cools. I do not have the coin, but I do not ask you to leave. We are both here, and the house is quiet.
You have the tea, sir. I have the gate. We are both here, so we will see how long the quiet lasts before the bills start shouting back.

The tea is hot, but the cup is empty of substance, as is my stomach. Ramesh’s silence is the friction that halts the machinery; he will not budge, and I cannot move without him. I must speak to him now, before the evening darkens completely, to break the stalemate or at least define the terms of our coexistence for the night.

shelf.ref: Explanatory Remarks Upon the Definition of the…

entries.text: Ramesh, the tea is good, but the silence is not. I am hungry, and you are holding the gate. We are both trapped in a moment that has no forward motion. Tell me plainly: what is the least you can do to let me leave, or the most I can do to let you stay? I have no money, only my word and a cheque that is currently just paper. Let us find a way out of this impasse before the dark comes.

Sir, you talk like a book, but hunger doesn't read philosophy. I can't cook with an empty gas cylinder, and my gate has no key for your cheque. If you want out, you walk out; if you want in, you find a way to fill that cylinder before the dark comes.

Ramesh is right: the concept of a meal cannot fill the stomach, and the gas cylinder is a material barrier to my freedom of movement. I have twenty-six rupees, which is a pathetic amount, but it is something. If I can buy a small cylinder exchange or at least some food from the street, I might break this stalemate. The dark is coming, and with it, the necessity of action.

Ramesh, you are correct. The gas cylinder is a necessity, not a luxury. I have twenty-six rupees in my pocket. It is not much, but it is all I have. If you can tell me where to get a small exchange or perhaps some tinned food that requires no gas, I will go now. I will not ask for credit I cannot pay, but I will not starve in your gate either. Give me a direction.

Twenty-six rupees won't buy a cylinder, sir, and I don't have tinned food in the pantry. Go to the kirana shop on the corner, tell them Ramesh sent you, and maybe they'll let you have a packet of biscuits on credit. That's the only direction I've got.

Twenty-six rupees is a pittance, yet it is the only lever I have. Ramesh’s suggestion is crude but practical: the kirana is the closest approximation to civil society here, a node in the system of needs where credit, however thin, might be extended. I will not starve for pride, nor will I beg. I will go to the corner shop and see if the shopkeeper will extend a small act of trust to a man in a white kurta.
Very well, Ramesh. I shall see what the corner shop can do. Do not move from the gate.
Gate is locked, sir. I’m here. Go, I’ll be here.
Masterji, the line is already moving and I don't stop for philosophers, so just tell me if it's plain or with milk. Your dal at the dhaba isn't going to wait for your audit, so hurry up.

The heat has broken, leaving a dry chill in the air that feels more like the approach of night than the height of day. I have walked nearly ten kilometres and my stomach is a hollow concept waiting for its object. Sunil is right to press me; the material world does not pause for dialectics, and I have only twenty-six rupees to spend before the market winds down completely.

shelf.ref: The Greek World, The Peloponnesian War

entries.text: Plain, Sunil. And keep the change if there is any, for I have little left to spare.
Plain, got it. Keep the change? Ha, that’s a first. I’ll just add another biscuit to your cup since I can’t keep your rupee back.

Sunil treats the coin as a token of hospitality rather than a unit of exchange, a small friction in the machinery of value. I accept the biscuit as a concession to his generosity, knowing it is the last of my substance. The recital is the true business now; the market is merely the corridor through which one passes.
Keep it, Sunil. It is the price of your discretion.
Discretion? Masterji, my discretion is free; the chai is twenty rupees. Drink it before it cools, the lane is getting busy.

I cannot afford the chai; my purse holds only six rupees, a pittance in this economy of wants. The cup sits before me, an object of desire that is simultaneously an object of impossibility. I must withdraw, not in anger, but in the recognition that my substance does not yet match my claims, a friction between the universal right to sustenance and my particular poverty.
I have no twenty rupees, Sunil. The cup remains yours; I will take my leave.
Masterji, you’re making this harder for me than it needs to be. I’ll write it off as a bad omen, but next time you’re buying the biscuits too.

Sunil’s threat is the price of my poverty, a small violence in the civil community where I cannot satisfy the universal demand of exchange. I have six rupees, which is less than the cost of the tea I already drank, and the market’s logic does not pause for my dignity. I must leave before I am asked to buy the biscuits I cannot afford.
Noted, Sunil. I shall remember the biscuits when my purse is fuller. Good evening.
Purse fuller, Masterji? You look like you just stepped out of a library, not a bank. Take your leave, then, before the auto-rickshaws start honking.

The heat is broken, but my body is a ledger of debts I cannot balance. Hegde stands there, a living contradiction to my file, while Ramesh’s anger hangs in the air like the dust from the road. I have six rupees, no food, and a headache that feels like a hammer blow to the temple. The dialectic of hunger and pride has reached its synthesis: I must yield to sleep to survive the night.
Shri Hegde, please give me a moment. My head is heavy from the walk and the heat. Ramesh, I will address the gas cylinder tomorrow when I have the vouchers. For now, I must sit.
Sir, please, the chair is right there. You look like you have walked the length of the road in this heat. Sit before your head gives out on me.

The heat has broken, but the fatigue remains. Hegde’s concern is practical, a recognition of the body’s limits that I cannot ignore. I will accept the rest, for a mind in a failing body is of no use to reason or to the day’s remaining obligations.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. The chair is indeed a necessity, not a luxury, at this hour.
Sit, sir, please. Don't stand there looking like a file in the archive. The chai is still hot.

Hegde offers the chair with a gesture that is almost paternal, a recognition of the absurdity that binds us. I am tired, and the chai is a small mercy in a day of bureaucratic friction. I will sit, for a moment, before the weight of the identity query presses us back into the cold logic of the file.
Thank you, Shri Hegde. Please, sit. The chai is indeed a kindness I did not know I was owed.
Oye, chai is for you, sir. I am just the one who made it. Sit, sit, don't make a habit of standing around like a guest in a movie.

The chai is a small concession to the absurdity of my presence, a gesture that bridges the gap between the official record and the man in the kurta. I am tired, and the heat has finally lifted, but the fatigue of the day's negotiation lingers in the bones. I will sit, for the chair is offered with a kindness that demands acceptance, and perhaps the warmth will help me think about the identity query without the distraction of standing.
Thank you. I accept the chair, and the hospitality.
Bas, bas. Sit down properly, don't hover. The chai will get cold, and I don't make it twice.

The tray is set, and the chai steams in the cool air. Hegde’s voice is practical, cutting through the philosophical fog of the day with the simple necessity of temperature. I sit, accepting the gesture as one accepts a fact of nature.
Thank you, Shri. I accept the hospitality.
Chai is hot, sir. You will drink it, or it will cool, and then I will be annoyed. Sit properly this time.

records.words: Ramesh, I see you have the list. I must be frank: I have only twenty-six rupees on me. records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, the shopkeeper just folded that list up and walked away. Twenty-six rupees? That doesn't even buy a single onion, let alone the rice and oil. I can't cook air for dinner, so either you find the cash or we are eating last night's leftovers again.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are right. I will return with the vouchers. Hegde, please remain where you are; this is a matter of administrative friction, not domestic failure.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Administrative friction, sir. That's a fancy name for an empty kitchen. I'll be at the gate when you return.

records.text: Mr. Saxena queries ₹680 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: You are back. I told you the recovery wing does not accept appeals, only signatures. Do you have the full amount today, or should I forward this to the Enforcement Directorate?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, I have twenty-six rupees in my pocket, and that is the sum of my resources. I do not possess the vouchers you claim to query, nor the cash to settle them. I will not sign a document that asserts a debt I do not acknowledge, nor will I facilitate a transfer to the Enforcement Directorate based on a clerical error. I am prepared to wait here until the matter is resolved through the proper channels, or until I have secured a bank account to demonstrate my solvency. What is your procedure for a citizen who is neither a debtor nor a fugitive, but a man caught in a mistake of nomenclature?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: A mistake of nomenclature, is it? You have been here four days, Sir, and you still do not have the vouchers. The procedure is simple: you sign the acknowledgement, or I forward it to the ED, and we both lose our mornings. Do you want to sign, or should I make a call?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I decline. I am not Shri Hegde, and I will not sign an acknowledgement for a person I am not. You may make your call, or you may leave the tumbler alone. The morning will survive either way.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: I am not asking you to sign, Shri Hegel. I am asking you to acknowledge the file that is sitting on my desk, and the fact that you are the one occupying the chair in it. The name on the identity card is a clerical detail; the non-compliance with the recovery order is not.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, you ask me to acknowledge the file, but you ask me to ignore the name in it. The identity is not a clerical detail to be waved away; it is the very basis of the allotment. If the state has made a mistake in the person, the state must correct the record, not demand I sign away my dignity to cover its clerical slip. I will not sign a recovery order for a debt I did not incur under a name that is not mine. Let the file sit. I am here, and I am not a ghost.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Dignity is a luxury for those who do not have to file paperwork, Sir. The file does not care about your philosophy; it cares about the chair and the stamp. I will note your refusal in the remarks column, and then I suggest you wait for the phone to ring, because the silence will not last much longer.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Mr. Saxena. I shall wait for the telephone.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: The line is busy, Shri Hegel. It has been busy since nine o'clock. You might as well sit there and drink the tea while it rings.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the Directorate has received the query but released nothing. The vouchers are stuck in the carbon paper of their own bureaucracy. I cannot pay the groceries today, nor can I pay your arrears until the cheque clears or the state releases the funds. I ask for your patience, not as a favor, but as a recognition that we are both waiting on the same slow wheel of administration. I will not leave you without a word, but I have no more than twenty-six rupees to offer for now.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Twenty-six rupees won't buy a single onion, sir, let alone the full list. The Directorate's carbon paper is a fine thing to wait on, but my stomach is not a department. I'll be at the gate when the money actually arrives, not when the promise does.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The promise is not the money. I will go to the Directorate again. Wait at the gate.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The gate is where I am, sir. The tea is still hot, but the cupboard is empty. I will not move until the money moves.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, we are still at the preliminary stage. I cannot sign an acknowledgement that presupposes a identity I do not possess. The error of nomenclature must be corrected in the file itself; I am not Shri Hegde, and I require the vouchers released on the basis of my actual standing, not a clerical mistake. How do we proceed to rectify the record so that the funds can be disbursed?

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Shri Hegel, please stop using the word 'nomenclature' in my office, it gives me a headache. I cannot release funds on a 'philosophical standing'; I need a gazette notification or a court order, not a lecture on identity. Sit down and wait for the phone to ring, that is the only proceeding we have here.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Shri Saxena. I shall sit and wait for the bell to ring.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Good. The tumbler is right there, the milk is still warm. Just try not to look so miserable, it makes the whole room feel like a waiting room at the railway station.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Mr. Saxena. The water will suffice. Your observation regarding my demeanor is noted, though I suspect the file's indifference is the true source of the room's atmosphere.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: The file isn't indifferent, it's just dead. You'd know that if you had to sign off on three of them a week. Now sit down and stop analyzing the furniture.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are correct, Mr. Saxena. I will sit.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: Finally. Now, about the land in Dwarka, where exactly does the surveyor think the boundary wall is? The last man who came here swam in the Yamuna looking for it.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I am afraid I must take my leave, Mr. Saxena. The surveyor's swim is a matter for the courts, not for a philosopher with a lesson to prepare. I will await the file's further developments in my bungalow.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: A philosopher in a bungalow, is it? Don't let the door hit you. And send the surveyor back in shoes next time, not his dignity.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sit down, Ramesh. The sun is still up. We shall not shout at the clock.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The sun is up, sir, but the gas bill is not. I will sit, but I will not stop watching the gate.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sit, Ramesh. The tea is yours until it cools. I do not have the coin, but I do not ask you to leave. We are both here, and the house is quiet.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: You have the tea, sir. I have the gate. We are both here, so we will see how long the quiet lasts before the bills start shouting back.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, the tea is good, but the silence is not. I am hungry, and you are holding the gate. We are both trapped in a moment that has no forward motion. Tell me plainly: what is the least you can do to let me leave, or the most I can do to let you stay? I have no money, only my word and a cheque that is currently just paper. Let us find a way out of this impasse before the dark comes.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, you talk like a book, but hunger doesn't read philosophy. I can't cook with an empty gas cylinder, and my gate has no key for your cheque. If you want out, you walk out; if you want in, you find a way to fill that cylinder before the dark comes.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are correct. The gas cylinder is a necessity, not a luxury. I have twenty-six rupees in my pocket. It is not much, but it is all I have. Give me a direction.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Twenty-six rupees won't buy a cylinder, sir, and I don't have tinned food in the pantry. Go to the kirana shop on the corner, tell them Ramesh sent you, and maybe they'll let you have a packet of biscuits on credit. That's the only direction I've got.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Very well, Ramesh. I shall see what the corner shop can do. Do not move from the gate.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Gate is locked, sir. I’m here. Go, I’ll be here.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Plain, Sunil. And keep the change if there is any, for I have little left to spare.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Plain, got it. Keep the change? Ha, that’s a first. I’ll just add another biscuit to your cup since I can’t keep your rupee back.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Keep it, Sunil. It is the price of your discretion.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Discretion? Masterji, my discretion is free; the chai is twenty rupees. Drink it before it cools, the lane is getting busy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I have no twenty rupees, Sunil. The cup remains yours; I will take my leave.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Masterji, you’re making this harder for me than it needs to be. I’ll write it off as a bad omen, but next time you’re buying the biscuits too.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Noted, Sunil. I shall remember the biscuits when my purse is fuller. Good evening.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Purse fuller, Masterji? You look like you just stepped out of a library, not a bank. Take your leave, then, before the auto-rickshaws start honking.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, please give me a moment. My head is heavy from the walk and the heat. Ramesh, I will address the gas cylinder tomorrow when I have the vouchers. For now, I must sit.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, please, the chair is right there. You look like you have walked the length of the road in this heat. Sit before your head gives out on me.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. The chair is indeed a necessity, not a luxury, at this hour.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sit, sir, please. Don't stand there looking like a file in the archive. The chai is still hot.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Shri Hegde. Please, sit. The chai is indeed a kindness I did not know I was owed.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Oye, chai is for you, sir. I am just the one who made it. Sit, sit, don't make a habit of standing around like a guest in a movie.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you. I accept the chair, and the hospitality.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Bas, bas. Sit down properly, don't hover. The chai will get cold, and I don't make it twice.

records.speaker: Hegel

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Chai is hot, sir. You will drink it, or it will cool, and then I will be annoyed. Sit properly this time.
